name: STAND-IN (synthetic) for NIH ChestX-ray14: workshop slice (200 chest radiographs)
description: SYNTHETIC STAND-IN, NOT DIAGNOSTIC. These are procedurally generated placeholder images, not radiographs: no NIH image is included. They stand in for the slice described below until the real files have been prepared, and the source and terms describe the dataset that will replace them. A 200-image slice of the NIH ChestX-ray14 collection, prepared for the December 2026 radiology workshop: frontal chest radiographs of adults, one per patient, balanced by sex and age band, at most 1024 px on the longest side. The reference labels of the evaluation task are held by the evaluation service and are not published. The reference label (airspace opacity present or absent) is invented for the stand-in and has no relation to the placeholder images. Source: https://nihcc.app.box.com/v/ChestXray-NIHCC. The images are provided by the NIH Clinical Center, which is the data provider. Cite: Xiaosong Wang, Yifan Peng, Le Lu, Zhiyong Lu, Mohammadhadi Bagheri, Ronald M. Summers. ChestX-ray8: Hospital-scale Chest X-ray Database and Benchmarks on Weakly-Supervised Classification and Localization of Common Thorax Diseases. IEEE CVPR 2017, pp. 3462-3471.
dct:rights: PLACEHOLDER, TO BE REPLACED: the README shipped in the NIH download has not been read yet, so its text is not recorded here. As reported by third parties quoting NIH (Google Cloud public-dataset page, read on 20 November 2026): no restrictions on the use of the images, with three attribution requirements, namely a link to the NIH download site, a citation of the CVPR 2017 paper and an acknowledgement that the NIH Clinical Center is the data provider. rai:dataCollection: Selection rule: 200 images drawn with a fixed seed (20261217) from the images of the metadata file that have a reference label, a patient aged 18 or over, sex recorded as F or M and a PA projection. Six strata (sex by age band: 18-39, 40-59, 60+) of equal size to within one image, 40% of each with the finding; at most one image per patient. 60 of them, with the same balance, form the reading subset.
